Ignore the previous negative reviews. These were before the XL update was released. 

The game is perfect now. Too bad most would have moved on to other fighting games like Tekken 7 and Injustice 2. Still a good game nonetheless. My only gripe is the lack of characters from the previous game (MK 9) and unplayable characters that you encounter in the story mode (i.e. Baraka, Sindel, Rain, Kabal, Nightwolf, Li Mei, etc).

I'm hoping one day Netherrealm Studios would release an MK game that boasts the complete roster ala MK: Armageddon from the PS2-era days.

HERE IS HOW TO FIX THE CRASHING PROBLEM, SERIOUSLY, READ BELOW!

1. Go to your library, click on MKX.
2. Locate the part that says "DLC", it should be right below the achievements.
3. You'll see Install pack 1 through 20 something.
4. Select all of them and they will begin to install manually.

The issue here was steam's pre-load feature, it had nothing to do with the actual MKX game, so don't blame the devs. If you really want to play at the moment, that's how you can do it. Also if you could upvote this so people know what to do, that'd be appreciated.

Mortal Kombat is one of those franchises I will always cherish.  That being said, the pricing model of this game is atrocious.  There are decisions I agree with - for example, offering to allow players to spend money to unlock all Krypt items.  Not everyone enjoys unlocking.  The biggest ones I disagree with are the way the characters are sold.  It's almost like the game wants to be a F2P with microtransactions, except that it's not F2P because you have to drop $60 to get in the door.  The Kombat Pack kind of sort of is like a Season Pass, except it isn't because it leaves out Goro.  So you've gotta drop your $60 for the game, another $30 for the Kombat Pack, and on top of that you also have to buy Goro.  I'm assuming that if they release any more characters, you'll have to buy them as well.  Unacceptable business practice in my opinion.  Either make the game free to play and then nickle and dime players for specific content, or put a price sticker on all of the content that we pay up front and then give us the content.  For this reason, I am going to have to say not recommending this game.  It's a shame too, because it's otherwise a fantastic game.  But I refuse to support this kind of greed.

I love this game. No, it's not my favorite in the series, and in all honesty, I never really bothered learning most of the moves for the ridiculously large cast of characters, let alone 3 distinct variations per character, and I always got my ass handed to me online as a result, well before it became a ghost town anyway. Nevertheless, the story mode is excellent, lots of really creative and bada*s new characters, the visuals and gory fatalities are top notch--pretty much unrivaled until of course MK11 came around, sound is great, and combat is fast and frenetic. Tower Ladders aren't as fun to play anymore as they were in MK9 (RIP if you missed your chance to buy it here on Steam) because Medium is too easy but Hard is way too B.S. hard. The Krypt is expanded upon, but it's got none of that RNG crap I hear MK11 is plagued with. Oh, and Brutalities make a return from UMK3, and there are really cool new stage fatalities.

So why a "DON'T RECOMMEND" when I sing this game praises? The file size. You see, WB decides to put banner ads in a $60 game, constantly telling you to buy the season pass. Since the game sells dirt cheap every sale, pretty much everyone owns the full MKXL version now, so they had to update the banner ads. Now they tell you to buy MK11. Those new banner ads, which have NO place in such a premium game to begin with, take up 40 GB of space!!! I sh*t you not, this game more than DOUBLED in file size from around 30-something GB to now well over 70 GB in just this last year. How? Why? I have no idea. But since Steam doesn't let you download past versions of a game like GOG Galaxy does, you either have to suck it up or uninstall the game. It will eat into your monthly data allowance or valuable hard drive space, in my case, the latter is more of a problem.

Moreover, the online is pretty much dead on PC ever since MK11 came out, and even before then most noobs (like me) would get destroyed because you're unlikely to find a match with a player of equal skill level.

Still, at the price it goes for, the game would be more than worth it for the singleplayer alone, doubly so if you got a friend and a controller for local play. Unfortunately I cannot play this game until they reverse whatever caused the file size to get so large, and consumers should not encourage this kind of behavior. So until they fix this, I'm going to keep a negative review, and that pains me, because I really do love MKX.

[b]New characters, finally[/b]

MK 9 was a great game but there were no real new characters in it. Plus, it was a sort of remake of the first 3 episodes. MK X finally sports completely new characters who debut here for the first time. Some of them are present thanks to their family: the daughter of Johnny and Sonya, Cassie Cage or Jacqui Briggs who decided to follow in the footsteps of his father, Jax. This also explains that some 20 years have since passed, hence the children joining the tournament. 

Once again we have a story mode full of cutscenes and a dozen chapters where each chapter gives us control of one individual. Again, we just take use of the good guys and our goal is to defeat Shinnok. The cutscenes look better than ever and quick time events regularly occur. Interestingly, just because we fail to quickly press the button appearing on screen it does not mean game over. Overall, this is an exciting story mode (with some dialogues being quite cheesy, though) and once you are done the many towers await to use the new roster consisting of 33 characters.

[b]Instead of X head for XL[/b]

A witty change to the title to indicate the presence of all DLCs. Some of the new characters, such as Goro, are available only if the related content is purchased. I recommend that you buy the XL version to have the full experience. Remember Freddy Krueger in MK 9? We now have 4 new characters joining from famous horror franchises: the silent Jason Vorhees, the crazy Leatherface, the alien xenomorph and the extra-terrestrial predator all join the battle. Their special attacks and fatalities are all similar to what they do in their respective films. 

[b]Interactions, Brutalities & cool dialogues[/b]

During the fight some of the background items can be used by just the press of a button. This means throwing objects at our enemies or when we are cornered our character can quickly climb up the wall and jump over their opponent. This means of an escape comes in handy especially on higher difficulties. It's a good idea to make use of the stages that are not just there to be showcases of the engine's capabilities. As for the engine: this latest Mortal Kombat still uses Unreal Engine 3.

In MK 9 they decided to include babalities beside the good old fatalities. In MK X there are Brutalities instead. These are fatalities that occur when we use a special affect as the last attack against our opponent. Instead of the A.I. yelling "Finish him / her" we immediately see a fatality. For instance, if we finish the last round with Cage's nut cracker special attack our enemy loses his head. There are also stage brutalities that require the stage interaction (those that cause damage) to be the last of our performance. Now, just because you use a special attack to perform a Brutality there are some pre-requisites to be met (a certain distance or number of usage of that attack during match etc.) 

My favourite part of MK X are the dialogues. Before the fight begins each character has to say something to the other. It is interesting for those that have a history (Scorpion and Sub-Zero) or for those that are close to one another (Johnny and Cassie). There are several dialogues for the same character combinations; my favourite is Cage yelling "It's Game Over Man!" when facing Alien. This is probably a reference to Bill Paxton's character, Hudson, in Aliens.

[b]For extra longevity: variations & factions[/b]

When picking a fighter you can choose from three variations. This affects the fighting style of that person. For instance, while Sub-Zero can use his signature ice ball attack all the time creating an ice clone is only possible under one variation. Under another the same button combination makes him use an ice hammer to smack his opponent. Some of the above-mentioned Brutalities require a specific variation. This feature is mainly new to the PC gamers as on console variations were present in previous MK titles. The robot characters have the cheapest variations of all: Cyrax, Sector, Smoke and Cyber Sub-Zero are considered variations under the character titled Triborg.

Let's talk about towers as there are many. The living towers change on an hourly and daily basis. These usually have an assortment of characters where during each fight a modifier is activated. This can be regeneration for you or extra damage output for your opponent or simply rockets falling from the sky causing damage that gradually increases as you make progress. "Test of Might" also returns and button smashing becomes a BIG PAIN if you want to destroy the last item on top.

Now, when you begin your journey with MK X the computer asks you to pick a faction. You recognise all 5 immediately: you know Sonya is part of Special Forces, Sub-Zero is a member of the Lin Kuei and Kano does his arms dealing via Black Dragon etc. Faction and War Towers will appear and even invasions: the latter means you have an extra fight while completing a random tower (these are labelled as assassinations), plus, you can attack a boss which is a randomly chosen character who always has his armour up. The idea here is to survive the longest and try to cause as much damage as possible.

Faction events last for a week all the time and those coming out as number one get extra rewards. Our contribution can be 1000 War Points daily; this we achieve by simply playing the game and completing towers. Also, there are Dragon Challenges: for instance, complete a round with a 10-hit combo or a health meter above 75%. We get XP for just about anything, plus, we also get koins as the Krypt function returns. This now looks much better and it has a lot of objects to interact with to find extra fight modifiers, concept / fan arts, fatalities (all brutalities are locked per default) etc. 

[b]Konclusion[/b]

MK X (but really just XL) is an excellent follow-up to MK 9 with new characters, exciting stages with the option to interact with items and, most of all, gory fatalities. Some of them looks truly disgusting due to the visible intestines. You need to have the stomach (pun intended) to bear witness to Kano's disembowelling his opponent or Ermac's little trick to create a pile of entrails. Oh, and if you think you were able to master MK 9 on very hard MK X will be surprisingly difficult once you leave the medium setting behind. The 10th MK game in the series is a (gory) blast, therefore, highly recommended!

[b]Mortal Kombat X is the latest entry in the MK franchise and boy, what a good game![/b]

I must confess that I stoped playing those games since MK 3 and only now decided to go back to them. Seems like Mortal Kombat 9 got criticized for its cartoonish character models, especially the female ones, so this time in MKX they tried a more realist approach, making characters look more like real people, with men looking not that buff and women looking not that busty. The result is that now the carnage has a real gory feeling, like if you are taking part in some kind of slasher movie, especially whe you perform one of the infamous fatalities and do crazy gory stuff with the opponent's body, like ripping their heart, cutting their head off and other even more macabre stuff.

[h1]Single Player[/h1]

There's a bunch of single player modes, so even if you don't play online you still gonna find the game fun anyways. The story mode in this game is kinda good, I mean, it makes sense and is entertaining enough without being too dumb. Thumbs up to Netherrealm for making a fighter with a decent story mode. The other single player modes are usually variations of the traditional "towers" found in usual Mortal Kombat games, and here you have a huge amout of those towers. The most fun are the so called "living towers" which provide you some kind of challege to increase the fight difficulty, like fighting while the screen is shaking or with lasers blasting both opponents and so on.

[h1]Online[/h1]

The only is kinda dead now, so you will only find random people to fight on weekends and such. Usually, to find an online partner, you have to call up someone on you friend list. That's how most of the online activity happens.

[h1]PC port[/h1]

It seems like when game was released, the netcode was broken and Netherrealm simply stopped caring about the PC version at all. Now all these problems were solved and the game runs fine on PC with all the content included.

[h1]Problems[/h1]

The problems with this game are only two, both gameplay releated:
1- Fireballs and long ranged attacks are too overpowered. You can pick up certain characters and keep basically running away while apamming fireballs and the opponent can do little about it. Unfortunately, this seems to be a recurrent problem in all Netherrealm recent fighters. See Injustice 1 and 2, for exemple.
2- The controls for the special moves are really messed up. Some follow the traditional MK style, like down, up + button, while others follow a more Street Fighter style, with quarter circle + button. I thinks it's time for MK to adopt only one style and get rid of this mess.

[b]Overall, it is a very good and solid fighter

I rate it 4.8/5.0[/b]

Unlees you lived under a rock last decades, you know what the Mortal Kombat is. So, I have no need to enter into detail about this good well-known button masher, I'll just name a quick list of pro's and cons, if you are interested to take some of your time to read it.

[b]Pros:[/b]

[list]
    [*]Good graphics, of course.
    [*]Good ambient and story. I do suggest you to try the story mode, it's pretty interesting.
    [*]Fast learning curve. You will spend most of your time on the floor, getting kicked in the head. But once you get a grip on controls, it's actually not that complicated to play the new MK. It's actually a bit easier than previous parts of the game.
    [*]Online matchmaking actually works. And I can't be more happy about it. Even though I got my аss kicked in my first 10 online matches, it's still good. Previos part of MK supported online game veeeery poorly. This one is fine.
    [*]It's a good game to play with your friends or alone, in your spare time. So, replayability value is good indeed.
    [*]You get to play as Predator, Alien, Jason or Leatherface, if you get the complete package (It's not so expensive, so I do recommend to get this version of the game from start).
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]

[list]
    [*]The game is slightly graphics-heavy. So you won't be able to play it on your grandma's toaster.
    [*]No chat or VoIp in online games, so you can't compliment or biтch-talk your opponent. But maybe it's a blessing in disguise.
    [*]Krypt. Yep... The Krypt. It's actually well-made and fun to explore, I compliment devs on that. But if you want to unlock new finishers for your fighters and stuff, oh boy... You are entering the world of pain and infinite grind. Ooor... You could buy it for a couple of bucks as a DLC. And I think it's a bit of a diск move from dev's part, but maybe it's just me. It's not expensive, though, if you are tired of trying to save some coins to open another daмn tomb.
    [*]Factions. Useless feature in my opinion. But it's just my opinion.
[/list]

So, yeah. I'd say that MKX is a good purchase and I do recommend you to buy it. You can play it on keyboard, if you do not have a controller. It's not that cosy, though, but possible. And if a price tag is a bit too much for you, wait for a sale and get it. You won't regret it. So, yeah... Good and fun game.

As a longtime Mortal Kombat fan, my journey with the series spans decades—from classic PlayStation battles to the early 3D iterations on PC, and now to the visually stunning Mortal Kombat X. While I initially hesitated due to the system requirements, I took the leap—and I’m glad I did. The game runs impressively well on high settings, delivering a sleek, modern interface and enhanced realism that elevates the experience.

The core battles are as intense and exhilarating as ever, with dynamic mechanics and visceral combat that showcase the franchise’s signature flair. The cinematic campaign is a standout, seamlessly blending gameplay with storytelling to create a movie-like experience. Exploring new heroes and their unique abilities added a fresh layer of excitement.

That said, Mortal Kombat X isn’t without its flaws. Offline play is smooth and enjoyable, but the online mode leaves much to be desired. Frequent slowdowns, freezes, and occasional crashes detract from the competitive multiplayer experience. Finding stable connections with other players is often a frustrating challenge. Another surprising issue is lag during character selection, even in offline mode. Oddly, the battles themselves run seamlessly, making the character-selection delay particularly baffling.

Despite these setbacks, Mortal Kombat X delivers an overall satisfying experience for fans and newcomers alike. The polished visuals, engaging campaign, and refined mechanics make it a worthy addition to the series. While optimization and multiplayer improvements are needed, I’m optimistic about potential updates. Here’s hoping the developers address these issues, ensuring the game reaches its full potential. Until then, happy fighting!

I know many don't appreciate long reviews but, it is necessary that I do so and go over some of the aspects of the game to remove your delimma of wether or not to buy this game.
Don't just go on the overall user reviews [u]as they don't always tend to some individual's personal choices.[/u]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay is very fast paced and fluid, one of the many perks I enjoy. It has strong flexible combat, oh my bad, [b]Kombat[/b], and no playable character is too overpowered so as to not being able to kounter attacks, or block,etc. Although you might find most of the people using Scorpion as it is one the most easiest to use among all other characters (also that it is a on the cover poster of the game). All the playable characters have 3 different sets (with the exception of Triborg having a fourth one), the overall gameplay of a charater is same but each of the character type provides enough variety to play with and experiment. According to me this game has very good replayability, as it will easily take 50+ hours or so to completely master a player that too not entirely and come to think of it there are 25 players (where Goro was a preorder bonus, now added DLC) +8 DLC characters. Also the new level interactions added are very fluid in movement and use. The online lobby is a bit empty now, quite obvious as this game is already 2 years old, and mostly with experienced players, so you might have a hard time winning an online match.

[b]X -Ray moves[/b]
The game has become quite famous because of the X-Ray moves, it is one of the example of the utter gruesomeness this game has to offer, if you have not seen a X-Ray move of this game before, I say you go and take a look on YouTube, if you are comfortable with it (or even enjoy it) this game will do you good. (Psst.. wanna learn skeleton structure and play at the same time, this game is your perfect goto guide)

[b]Fatality/Brutality[/b]
Here we come to the most important part of the game, the finishers - Fatality/Brutality (Brutality has been added in this edition and did not exist earlier). This part of the game in its first installment was responsible for the birth of the ESRB rating. Although it were sprites that were used back then, now it is rendered graphics (And boy it looks yummy!), Go  check it out first if you haven't already, it is excessively gruesome. If you love it, don't read much further buy the game!(well do read cause you might not find paying for additional players satisfactory) The fatality is quite easy to execute compared to the brutality which require a sequence of moves to be done during the duration of the match in order to execute it successfully, but boy it is satisfactory.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The game graphics are just marvelous, very realistic, bearing in mind it came out in 2015 (Please do not compare this statment to Crysis 3) The level design is very well done and the whole level as a good depth to itself. Even the texture details are well done. Also any blood splattered on the floor of the arena well be there till the end of the match. Compared to MK9 the human body is much more proportionate in this edition of the game. I recommend having a decently powerful machine (Please do not use a Potato PC) to enjoy the fluidity this game has to offer. Although it sucks that the game is locked in 60FPS.

[h1]DLC[/h1]
I wouldn't say much over this point, but I would suggest that you buy the DLCs during the sale if you really want. I hate the fact that the MK frachise is trying to milk this game for money with DLC characters, so not happy here!

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
I really don't know what to say, if you enjoy fluid, fast, and gruesome gameplay, this is meant for you. If not then I really don't recommend it for you as you might just end up throwing up your intestines (actually happens in a Fatality)!

Mortal Kombat X is the 10th installment in the iconic Mortal Kombat series, and probably the best game out of them all. It features 26 playable characters (35 if you include all the DLC) with each characters having 3 different variations that are designed to fulfill specific roles (zoning, trapping, rushdown and so on). The variations provide changes in terms of moves and combos, so in reality you're looking at a game with potentially 105 characters (DLC included), which is a lot. The characters are well balanced for the most part, which means whichever character you choose to main will probably also be tournament viable if you get good enough at the game.

The game is also very fast paced for a fighting game, and offers players tons of content, from a (good, but short) story mode; to traditional towers in which the player has to beat a series of AI opponents with a final boss at the top; to living towers (regular towers that get updated with new challenges every once in a while to mix things up) and more casual game modes such as test your might and test your luck. It also features a return of the Krypt, in which you can unlock various costumes, fatalities and other behind the scenes novelties.

This port had a rocky start when it first launched on PC, with people not being able to get past the main menu due to its many issues, but most of the issues it had are now fixed. All in all, the game continues Netherealm Studios' tradition of offering the player great value for money by showering him with tons of quality content - a lot more than what you'll find in any other fighting game out there.

So why am I not recommending this?

As of January 20th, Netherealm had announced that they are dropping support for Mortal Kombat X on the PC. This means that the Kombat Pack 2 DLC, featuring Triborg, Bo Rai Cho, Leatherface and Xenomorph, will not be released on PC at all. This also means that PC users will not get the updated netcode that is currently being developed for the console users, and will have to stick to the inferior (and quite horrible) netcode the game currently has. On top of all that, every new balance patch the game receives from now on will not make it to the PC. In sum, anyone who plays this game on PC is doomed to play an inferior and different game than the console version. You'll have less characters, worse online, and worst of all - the frame data on your moves list will not be compatible to the frame data of your console counterparts, which means that any effort of friendly competitive play between a PC user and a console user will automatically put the PC user at a disadvantage (if you had plans to play this game competitively in casual tournamens like I had, you might as well forget about it).

Now lets be clear: while I do hold Netherealm Studios responsible for this to some extent, in my book the main villain of this is Warner Brothers, who now demonstrate a pattern of releasing shoddy game ports on PC (Batman: Arkham Knight, anyone?) followed by quickly dropping support for said ports. That company proves time and time again that it doesn't care about PC consumers by outsourcing games to bad port developers and quickly dropping support for said ports in favor of making new DLC. This is quite embarrassing for the company, as it turns away from the few people still willing to give it money for its horrible PC releases.

If you're a fan of Mortal Kombat, consider buying it on console as it is indeed a good game. If you're strictly a PC user, however, don't bother. You'll be playing an inferior product that will be vastly different from the main game. Also, in the future, if you encounter a Warners Brothers game that is being ported to the PC - avoid it like the plague. I know I will.

Mortal Kombat X promised an exciting return to the brutal, over-the-top fighting action the series is known for, but sadly, it falls short in many areas. While the game retains the signature violence and gore the series is famous for, it is plagued by numerous issues that severely hinder the experience. Despite its flashy visuals and new characters, Mortal Kombat X feels more like a missed opportunity than a worthy addition to the franchise.

Why Mortal Kombat X Disappoints
🥊 Unbalanced Combat
One of the most frustrating aspects of Mortal Kombat X is its unbalanced combat system. While the game introduces new characters and variations for each fighter, some of these variations feel overpowered, while others seem useless. This creates an experience where certain characters dominate while others are left at a disadvantage, making it feel unfair and unpolished. The lack of balance leads to a predictable meta, with players often relying on a few “best” characters, which takes away from the game's overall diversity and fun.

🎮 Buggy Online and Matchmaking
Mortal Kombat X's online matchmaking is severely flawed, with players often facing long waiting times and connectivity issues. The netcode can be erratic, leading to laggy matches that ruin the competitive experience. Additionally, the matchmaking system itself feels flawed, with players frequently facing opponents who are either too easy or too difficult for their skill level, making it hard to enjoy the game consistently.

💰 Microtransactions and Grinding
Like many modern games, Mortal Kombat X includes microtransactions for cosmetic items, such as character skins and costumes. While this is common in the industry, Mortal Kombat X goes a step further by locking key content behind a paywall, forcing players to either spend money or grind for hours to unlock certain features. This pay-to-progress model detracts from the fun and creates a sense of frustration for players who just want to enjoy the game.

👹 Repetitive Story Mode and Lack of Innovation
The story mode in Mortal Kombat X is another letdown. While it tries to offer an engaging narrative, the story ultimately feels predictable and repetitive, with few surprises or significant twists. Additionally, the game doesn’t innovate much beyond the previous entries in terms of gameplay mechanics. The series' iconic fatalities and finishing moves are still present, but the lack of true innovation makes Mortal Kombat X feel like an iteration rather than a groundbreaking new release.

Conclusion
Mortal Kombat X had the potential to be a fantastic entry in the series, but a combination of unbalanced gameplay, technical issues, and grinding mechanics makes it hard to recommend. While the flashy fatalities and brutal combat remain intact, the game's flaws drag down the experience. For fans of the franchise, there are still enjoyable moments, but it’s difficult to look past the many issues that hinder its enjoyment. 3/10—a disappointing addition to an otherwise great series.

The content is wonderful; that isn't the issue... The issue is the complete absence of character balancing and juggling gone completely off the rails. I know every fighter, and can execute almost all of their moves, but this game has serious issues when it comes to juggling. A better name for MKX would be 'Juggling Abuse Simulator,' because that's all every fight boils down to in the end. Some characters don't heavily rely on juggling, but they have absolutely no chance of beating those who do. 

For those not familiar with juggling, it is a method of keeping your opponent in the air for as long as possible, and being able to attack them without them being able to do anything to counter it. You only have one way to escape a juggle in MKX, which is your two bar EX breaker, but it won't help. The worst players in the world will spend their entire lives coming up with the lamest combos imaginable, ones that offer you absolutely no way out, and have infinite resets, so that when you DO finally hit the ground, they have a 50/50% chance of starting the combo on you once again. Since some of these ridiculous combos end up doing 50% damage... you can get the picture... That's basically it. I really like the game's content overall, and the fighting system is extremely fun... until you end up facing a juggle whore, and you simply have no chance of winning unless you juggle whore them back... and I'd rather be doing something better with my time. Personally, when I do one of these combos on another player, I feel like a complete jerk, because I know how messed up it is, but don't expect anyone online to admit it. 

So, if you wanna drop a lot of money to have a good time... for a while... then go for it. I have certainly had my share of fun, but if you think you're going to use skill and actual fighting to win fights against juggle whores... think again. A prime example of this problem is Kotal Kahn compared to Takeda. Kotal has very slow attacks, and a slow projectile, but his combos do massive damage, as he is extremely difficult to use until you learn his moves. He is well designed. Takeda, on the other hand, has a lightning fast teleport, whips that can strike you and open combos on the other side of the stage, very fast, HUGE juggling combos, and a lightning fast low projectile. It gets old after a while, as the game allows you no way to defeat a character that laughably unbalanced unless you do the same thing. Mortal Kombat X is a hard-hitting fighting game that combines exceptionally violent spectacle with a combat system that has considerably more depth than its gruesome reputation might suggest. Developed by NetherRealm Studios, with QLOC involved in the PC version, and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment, the game builds upon the familiar foundations of the series while introducing mechanics that give every fighter additional tactical flexibility. Its mixture of fast battles, cinematic presentation, varied characters, extensive single-player content, and competitive multiplayer makes it an entertaining package even years after its original arrival.

The fighting system is easily its greatest strength. Battles move at a brisk pace, with punches, kicks, throws, special attacks, enhanced moves, environmental interactions, and lengthy combos producing an aggressive rhythm. Controls are accessible enough for newcomers to perform recognizable special moves relatively quickly, but becoming genuinely skilled requires considerably more practice. Timing, spacing, blocking, counterattacks, meter management, combo execution, and understanding an opponent's habits all become increasingly important. This balance between accessibility and complexity gives casual players immediate entertainment while leaving dedicated competitors with plenty to master.

One of the game's most important additions is the variation system. Each fighter can use different variations that modify abilities and encourage distinct strategies. Rather than simply choosing a character, players effectively choose a particular interpretation of that character. One variation may emphasize close-range pressure while another provides stronger ranged attacks, defensive techniques, weapons, or specialized combo opportunities. This greatly expands the strategic possibilities of the roster and encourages experimentation. Even after becoming comfortable with one fighter, learning another variation can noticeably change how that character approaches a match.

The roster offers a satisfying mixture of recognizable veterans and newer fighters. Familiar characters retain the moves and personalities that make them immediately identifiable, while newcomers help move the universe beyond relying entirely on nostalgia. Different body types, weapons, supernatural abilities, movement styles, and variation-specific techniques create meaningful distinctions between combatants. Finding a favorite character is relatively easy, but mastering several fighters can consume dozens of hours because each demands different approaches to offense and defense.

The cinematic story mode gives solo players a structured introduction to much of the roster. Instead of presenting a simple ladder of unrelated opponents, the campaign uses cutscenes and character-focused chapters to connect fights into a larger supernatural conflict. The narrative is intentionally exaggerated, combining family drama, rivalries, monsters, martial arts, otherworldly realms, and enormous threats. It may not be the primary reason competitive players return, but it provides entertaining context for the battles and gives newcomers an opportunity to try characters they might otherwise ignore.

Mortal Kombat's trademark brutality reaches extraordinary levels here. X-Ray attacks provide graphic demonstrations of bones breaking and internal injuries, while Fatalities turn victories into elaborate displays of exaggerated gore. These sequences are technically impressive and often creatively absurd, but the intensity of the violence means the game clearly is not intended for everyone. Players uncomfortable with graphic dismemberment, blood, and gruesome finishing moves will find very little effort has been made to soften the experience. For its intended audience, however, this unapologetic excess contributes strongly to the game's distinctive identity.

Visually, the darker artistic direction complements the violent atmosphere. Arenas contain substantial environmental detail, characters look appropriately battered during fights, and attacks carry convincing visual weight. Animation makes heavy strikes feel powerful rather than weightless, while environmental interactions add another layer of spectacle. Sound effects reinforce every major impact with appropriately exaggerated force, and the music supports the threatening atmosphere without overwhelming the action. Together, these elements make even ordinary matches feel dramatic.

There is also considerable replay value beyond completing the campaign. Towers, challenges, character experimentation, unlockable content, achievements, local matches, and competitive play encourage repeated sessions. Local multiplayer remains particularly enjoyable because Mortal Kombat works naturally as a game where two players can immediately start fighting without needing a lengthy setup. Online competition provides a much steeper challenge, especially when facing experienced players capable of executing optimized combos and exploiting matchup weaknesses. The learning curve becomes substantially harsher at that level, but improvement can also be extremely satisfying.

On Steam Deck, Mortal Kombat X is Steam Deck Verified. The handheld format suits the game's relatively self-contained matches particularly well, allowing players to work through fights, practice characters, or tackle single-player activities without needing a desktop setup. Controller-oriented combat also translates naturally to the Deck's built-in controls. As with any competitive fighting game, players seeking the most precise experience may still prefer a dedicated controller or fighting stick, but the Deck provides a convenient way to experience the game portably.

The game does have weaknesses. The variation system can initially complicate character selection, and players interested primarily in casual fighting may never fully appreciate its deeper mechanics. The extreme violence also limits its audience by design. Furthermore, competitive fighting games naturally become less forgiving as skill levels rise, so newcomers entering serious matches can encounter opponents with dramatically greater knowledge. None of these issues fundamentally damage the excellent core combat, but they influence what kind of player will get the most value from the experience.

Mortal Kombat X ultimately delivers much more than shock value. Its brutal finishing moves provide the recognizable spectacle, but the responsive fighting mechanics, character variations, diverse roster, cinematic campaign, competitive possibilities, and substantial replayability form the foundation that keeps it engaging. It successfully accommodates quick casual battles while providing enough mechanical sophistication to reward players willing to study individual characters and improve their execution. For fans of aggressive fighting games who have no objection to graphic violence, it remains a highly entertaining and mechanically rewarding entry in the series.

And play Mortal Kombat X! Scorpion says it best, and should entice both newcomers to fighting games and MK veterans. As someone who played the previous Mortal Kombat game, I can testify that the fighting system and feel of the moves is much more robust and improved. This is a game that has been well-worked on and refined to allow for precise and feel-good execution of moves. I cannot recommend it enough.

COMPLAINTS ABOUT MULTIPLAYER SLOWNESS CANNOT BE APPLIED TO ALL USERS. It is incredibly variable and mostly dependent on individual internet capabilities, and widespread lag has been greatly reduced since the first few weeks.

In addition to gameplay mechanics, MKX features a wide variety of specializable characters that allow for a new fight every time. All 25-odd Non-DLC characters feature 3 different variations, essentially giving the game 100 different play-styles if all DLC is acquired. Each character has unique dialogue, and if Scorpion is fighting Mileena, he will refer to her by name or trait in one of several intros. It is remarkable that a game with such exceptional gameplay has such strong characters as well, but you can believe that you will find at lease 6 characters unbelievably bad-ass in some way.

I play Liu Kang almost exclusively. He has three variations, each giving him different special moves and essentially redefining his playstyle. Each variation also gives him a slightly new skins. He also has a number of skins purchasable or obtainable through gameplay. He has hundreds of lines of dialogue and his character model looks and behaves great. I only play one character and still have a blast with MKX.

If you can afford it or catch it on sale, MKX is fun for all and replayable for hours, online or offline. If you are not very good, playing against easy bots offline is still fun and will refine your reflexes and skills quickly. The revolutionary practice mode is difficult to explain but impressive and remarkably useful. If you have any doubts, check out the Mortal Kombat Community channel on YouTube for some cool trailers and character breakdowns.

1. Pick an easy character to start with. Scorpion is great, as is Sub-Zero
2. Some projectiles will hit you if you crouch-duck but not if you simply duck
3. Don't button-mash, don't projectile-spam, and BLOCK
